title: Substitute string and token variables in tree templates
body:
`TemplateConf.test_var()` recognizes variables represented by strings, tokens, or `var` trees. Matching already supports all three forms, but `apply_vars()` only substitutes tree nodes. A grammar that inlines its variable rule therefore leaves `$value` in the translated output, even though matching found the correct binding. Missing bindings for those variables also go unnoticed.

Recognize variables before descending into their children, following the matching logic. Reuse the bound tree directly, and retain the existing missing-variable error. Non-variable branches still use the normal transformer traversal.

Regression tests cover string/token/tree variables, nested and root variables, recursive-tree depth compatibility, unchanged templates and metadata, opaque replacement values, missing bindings, and translation with an actual grammar that inlines variable tokens.

- Five regression subcases fail on unchanged source and pass with this fix.
- Final complete suites: 1,342 / 1,334 tests, with the same 148 skips. Python 3.10 executes all Nearley tests with pinned Js2Py 0.68; upstream omits that module on Python 3.12 because the dependency cannot import there.
- Pinned mypy 1.12, all applicable pre-commit hooks, coverage run, documentation build, source/wheel builds, and CRLF-aware whitespace checks pass. Documentation retains its 23 existing warnings.

title: Respect tab stops in Python indentation
body:
PythonIndenter counts every tab as eight columns, even after preceding spaces. Python advances tabs to the next eight-column boundary instead. This causes the bundled Python parser to reject CPython-valid nested suites whose indentation mixes spaces and tabs.

Add a protected indentation-width hook and override it in PythonIndenter using `expandtabs`. Keep generic Indenter's existing fixed-width behavior and preserve source token values/positions. This does not add CPython's separate inconsistent-tab validation.

title: Preserve optional placeholders when collapsing ambiguities
body:
With the default `maybe_placeholders=True`, absent optional children appear as `None` in parse trees. `CollapseAmbiguities` passes those placeholders directly to its Cartesian-product helper and raises `AssertionError`, including on `start: [WORD]` empty input and on genuinely ambiguous trees.

Treat each `None` placeholder as one possible child value before combining alternatives. Regression coverage includes all three Earley lexers, absent/present slots, placeholder-disabled controls, nested optional children, independent ambiguity combinations, metadata, and unchanged input trees.

title: Normalize the selected start rule in Nearley conversion
body:
Nearley rule definitions and references already pass through `_get_rulename()`, but the emitted parser start only receives an `n_` prefix. Generated parsers therefore fail to load when the selected rule needs case normalization, dollar escaping, or the special `_`/`__` conversion.

Use the existing name conversion for the selected start. This bundles all affected name forms in one fix. Regressions verify the selected non-first rule accepts the intended input and rejects the first rule's input.

title: Fix example error matching with unequal accepted tokens
body:

Use a nonnumeric state placeholder and lazy logging arguments. Matching behavior itself is unchanged. title: Preserve lexer positions with global DOTALL flags
body:
`g_regex_flags=re.DOTALL` lets regex terminals consume newlines, but the basic lexer's newline detection currently only inspects pattern text. Parsing `a\nb!` with `/a.*?b/` therefore reports the following token at line 1, column 4 instead of line 2, column 2. Ignored tokens, propagated tree spans, and subsequent error locations are affected too.

Pass the global flags into newline detection. Add regression coverage for retained and ignored terminals, text and bytes, combined flags, consecutive newlines/CRLF, source spans and tree metadata, errors, and compressed/uncompressed standalone parsers. Existing behavior without global flags is preserved.

title: Isolate tree metadata when making a deep copy
body:
`copy.deepcopy(tree)` currently reuses the original `Meta` object. Updating a copied parse tree's source location or an annotation consequently changes the original tree as well. Metadata references to the tree also keep pointing at the original.

Deep-copy metadata with the same memo used for children. Register the new tree in that memo before copying either field, so shared subtrees, shared metadata and metadata references back to the tree retain their relationships within the copied graph.

title: Fix context positioning for unexpected end of input
body:
`UnexpectedEOF.get_context()` currently interprets the end-of-input sentinel `-1` as a Python slice index. This puts the caret before the final character for short inputs, shows the wrong line after a trailing newline, and can omit the end of long inputs entirely.

Normalize that sentinel to the length of the supplied input before computing the context window. All nonnegative positions and missing positions retain their existing behavior.

Add three regression/control methods with 29 subcases covering empty input, multiline input, trailing newlines, tabs, bounded and zero spans, text and bytes, and actual errors from all three Earley lexers.

title: Preserve immutable parser snapshots when resuming parsing
body:
`ImmutableInteractiveParser.resume_parse()` currently advances the original parser and lexer state. Resuming the same snapshot twice therefore raises `UnexpectedToken` on the second call, and an unsuccessful parse also consumes the snapshot.

Resume through a mutable copy so that the snapshot remains reusable while preserving the existing return value. Regression tests cover both LALR lexers, snapshots before/during/after token consumption, unsuccessful parses, and generated standalone parsers.

Validation: full Python 3.10 suite (1,192 passed, 148 existing configuration skips; 1,340 total), plus 30 passing subtests, mypy, all pre-commit hooks, documentation build, and sdist/wheel build. The documentation build retains its 23 pre-existing warnings.

title: Visit shared subtrees before their parents
body:
`Tree.iter_subtrees()` reverses breadth-first discovery order, which can put a shared child after one of its parents when the child is reachable at different depths. This breaks bottom-up `Visitor` callbacks on real ambiguous parse trees. For example, `start: branch | leaf`, `branch: leaf`, `leaf: "a"` with explicit ambiguity visits `branch` before its shared `leaf`.

Deduplicate discovery by node identity, preserve the exact existing order for ordinary trees, and order shared dependencies before parents using an iterative pass. This also avoids repeatedly expanding queued shared nodes. Regression tests cover shared nodes, distinct equal nodes, unchanged ordinary-tree ordering, Visitor and Transformer behavior, and actual ambiguous parse output. Existing eager-snapshot and cycle-termination behavior is retained.

Validation:
- Original regression run: 3 failures and 2 errors
- Full Python 3.10 suite: 1,344 tests; Python 3.12 suite: 1,336 tests. Both retain the same 148 existing skips. Python 3.10 includes all Nearley tests, which the project's pinned Js2Py omits on 3.12.
- Pinned mypy, every configured pre-commit hook, and Sphinx HTML build pass (23 pre-existing documentation warnings).
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent checks covered 65,536 six-node ordered DAGs, 1,000 ordinary trees with exact previous identity order, standalone parsers, and a 20,001-node stress case.

Local benchmarks preserve/improve ordinary-tree timings. Correct DAG dependency ordering adds overhead, about 2.3–2.6x in the measured small/medium cases. Both paths are iterative and linear in vertices plus edges.

title: https://github.com/lark-parser/lark/pull/1665
body:
Fixes #1300.

## Problem

The tree matcher currently decides whether a `?rule` was inlined from the number of grammar symbols in its expansion. An underscored rule can contribute zero, one, or several children after tree shaping, so that count can differ from the actual number of children.

For example, reconstructing `f('a', 'b', [])` with the Python grammar produces `f('a''b',[],)`, merging the first two arguments. A minimal `?concat: item+` grammar also fails to reconstruct retained `concat` nodes with multiple children.

## Changes

This change keeps the ordinary rules for matching retained nodes and restricts inline alternatives to exactly one shaped child. It computes which hidden rules can contribute zero or one child, specializes those rules as needed, and preserves their original reconstruction callbacks so discarded tokens are restored in the right places.

Regression coverage includes `+` and `*` repetitions, hidden template rules, mandatory discarded prefix/suffix tokens, empty/multiple-child cases, and Python string arguments/concatenation. The new regressions fail on the unchanged upstream revision and pass with the fix.

## Validation

Tested in a Linux cloud environment:

- Python 3.12.14: `python -m tests`, 1,332 tests, 148 skips
- Python 3.13.5: `python -m tests`, 1,332 tests, 181 skips (optional dependencies not installed for this interpreter)

The Nearley import tests could not run: the pinned Js2Py 0.68 dependency raises a Python-bytecode compatibility error on Python 3.12. Other supported Python versions and operating systems have not been tested locally.

title: Fix Token inequality to respect token types (breaking change)
body:
`Token.__eq__` compares both the token type and string value, but `Token` inherits `str.__ne__`, which only compares the string value. Both `==` and `!=` can consequently return `False` for the same pair of tokens:

```python
from lark import Token

name = Token('NAME', 'if')
keyword = Token('KEYWORD', 'if')
assert not (name == keyword)
assert name != keyword  # Fails before this change
```

This affects filtering actual parse results. For a contextual LALR grammar with `start: KEYWORD NAME`, `KEYWORD: "if"`, and `NAME: /[a-z]+/`, parsing `if if` produces a keyword followed by a name. Filtering out `Token('KEYWORD', 'if')` with `!=` currently removes both tokens.

Add `Token.__ne__` that delegates to `__eq__`, preserves `NotImplemented` for reflected comparisons, and otherwise inverts the equality result. Comparisons with ordinary strings, position-independent equality, and the existing string hash remain unchanged.

The regression tests cover both operand orders, equal and different token types/values, strings and unrelated objects, positional metadata and hashing, reflected comparison results, subclass equality, and filtering parsed tokens.

Validation on exact base `9a4fb9c7458e8155636773a3cded0016d52516da`:

- New regression tests: three failures on unchanged source, all pass after the fix.
- Python 3.10.21: complete `python -m tests -v`, 1,342 tests, OK (148 existing skips); all eight Nearley tests run and pass.
- Python 3.12.14: complete `python -m tests -v`, 1,334 tests, OK (148 existing skips). The project itself omits the eight Nearley tests because pinned Js2Py 0.68 does not support this Python version.
- Clean-base comparison: 1,337 / 1,329 tests respectively, with the same 148 skips and the same Python 3.12 Nearley omission. No new skips, exclusions, or disabled backends.
- Pinned mypy 1.12.0: no issues in 34 source files.

title: Fix repeated variable bindings in tree templates
body:
Repeated occurrences of a tree-template variable currently overwrite each other. A pattern such as `pair($x, $x)` therefore matches different children and can rewrite the tree using only the second value.

Reject a match when an already-bound variable receives a different subtree. Equal trees still match. The regression tests cover sibling and nested conflicts, search, and translation.

title: separate tokens that would lex as one in Reconstructor.reconstruct
body:
1. `Reconstructor.reconstruct` puts a space between two emitted items only when the first one ends and the second one starts with an identifier character, so any other pair that concatenates into a different token is written with nothing between them.
2. The output then lexes differently from the tree it came from, so a parse/transform/write-back pass can quietly change the meaning of what it emits. With `COMMENT: /--[^\n]*/` in the grammar, the tree of `1 - -2` reconstructs to `1--2`, and reparsing that gives back just `1`, since the rest of the line is now a comment. `"<"` followed by `"="` becoming `<=`, and `"/"` followed by `"*"` opening a block comment, are the same defect.
3. Reading the pair back with a scanner over the grammar's own terminals, ordered the way the basic lexer orders them, and inserting the space when the first token's match would reach past its own end. The identifier test stays as the cheap first check and as the fallback for a boundary the scanner can't resolve, so a space is only added where the output did not read back correctly before.

I kept the fix in `reconstruct` rather than leaving it to `postproc`, since a caller writing its own spacing has no way to know which pairs the grammar lets run together.

Validation: full suite green (1330 tests, also under `pytest`), mypy clean, and the added `test_adjacent_tokens_lexing_as_one` fails on master and passes here. The check costs roughly a microsecond per token boundary: on a 10 KB JSON tree that is 3360 boundaries and about 3 ms against ~125 ms of reconstruction, and it is skipped entirely for the identifier pairs that already got a space. `examples/advanced/reconstruct_python.py` passes and fails on exactly the same hash seeds as before, since it does its own spacing in `postproc` (#1300).

title: Reject a TextSlice end that is outside the text

title: TextSlice accepts an end past the text
body:
**Describe the bug**

`TextSlice("hello", 0, 100)` succeeds and `len` is 100. `TextSlice("hello", 0, -100)` builds a slice whose length is negative. The docstring says an out of bounds start or end raises `AssertionError`. A negative start already does. `TextSlice("hello", 1, -1)` should stay start 1, end 4, length 3.

**To Reproduce**

```python
from lark.utils import TextSlice
print(len(TextSlice("hello", 0, 100)))
```

title: feat: add support for 'a' (ASCII) and 'L' (LOCALE) regex flags
body:
Reopens the work from #1655 (closed; head branch was deleted, so GitHub cannot reopen it).

Adds support for the `a` (ASCII/re) and `L` (LOCALE) regex flags in grammar token patterns.

### Changes
- `lark/load_grammar.py`: allow `a` and `L` in `_RE_FLAGS`; reject combining `a` and `u` (they are mutually exclusive) with a clear `GrammarError`
- `lark/lark.py`: validate flag/pattern compatibility at construction time:
  - `use_bytes=True` → reject the `u` (UNICODE) flag
  - str mode → reject the `L` (LOCALE) flag (in Python 3, `L` only works on bytes patterns)
- `lark/lexer.py`: under `use_bytes`, compile final regexps as bytes so `L` validates correctly
- `lark/utils.py`: `get_regexp_width` strips the `(?L:` group wrapper (width is unaffected; `sre_parse` rejects `L` on str patterns)
- Self-hosted grammars (`lark.lark`, `template_lark.lark`) accept the new flags
- Docs updated (`docs/grammar.md`) with the new flags and their constraints
- Tests: flag ordering with new flags, `a`/`u` conflict, ASCII flag behavior, `L` requiring `use_bytes`, `L` working with bytes input

### Notes for reviewers
The previous PR's CI failures could not be reproduced or inspected (logs unavailable), but this branch was verified locally with mypy 1.12 (clean) and the full test suite on Python 3.8 and 3.14 (all passing).

title: feat: add support for 'a' (ASCII) and 'L' (LOCALE) regex flags
body:
## Summary

Adds support for the `a` (ASCII) and `L` (LOCALE) regex flags in Lark grammars, closing #1527.

Beyond adding the flags to `_RE_FLAGS`, this PR makes them safe to use: flag combinations are validated at grammar-compile time with clear `GrammarError`s, the `L` flag works end-to-end with bytes lexers, the self-hosted grammars accept the new flags, the flags are documented, and the tests verify the actual ASCII/LOCALE semantics rather than just successful compilation.

## Changes

**Grammar parsing** (`lark/load_grammar.py`)
- `_RE_FLAGS` now includes `a` and `L`, so `/regex/a`, `/regex/L`, `"select"i`-style flag suffixes accept them
- Using `a` and `u` on the same literal raises a clear `GrammarError` (they are mutually exclusive in `re`)

**Validation** (`lark/lark.py`)
- `L` requires `use_bytes=True` — in Python 3 the LOCALE flag is only valid for bytes patterns; previously this crashed with a cryptic `re.PatternError` deep inside `re.compile`
- `u` with `use_bytes=True` raises a clear error for the equivalent reason

**Lexer plumbing** (`lark/lexer.py`, `lark/utils.py`)
- `BasicLexer` validates terminal patterns in their final form (bytes under `use_bytes`), so `(?L:...)` patterns compile cleanly
- `get_regexp_width` neutralizes `(?L:` before handing the pattern to `sre_parse`, which rejects it on str patterns (flags don't affect match width, so this is safe)
- `Pattern._get_flags` already sorts flags, so `a`/`L` combine deterministically with the existing flags

**Self-hosted grammars**
- `lark/grammars/lark.lark` and `examples/advanced/template_lark.lark` REGEXP terminals updated to `[imsluxaL]*`

**Docs** (`docs/grammar.md`)
- Flag list updated to `imsluxaL`, with notes on `a`/`u` exclusivity and the bytes-only requirement of `L`

## Testing

New and strengthened tests:
- `test_flag_order_with_new_flags` — `a` and `L` sort deterministically (`(?a:(?L:x))`), including with `use_bytes`
- `test_conflicting_ascii_unicode_flags` — `a` + `u` raises `GrammarError`
- `test_token_flags_ascii` — proves ASCII semantics: `/\w+/a` rejects `é`, while the same pattern without the flag matches it
- `test_token_flags_locale_requires_bytes` — `L` without bytes raises `GrammarError`
- `test_token_flags_locale_bytes` — `/\w+/L` with `use_bytes=True` parses bytes input

Full suite: `pytest tests/` → 1213 passed, 148 skipped. `mypy` (as run by `tox -e type`) and the pre-commit hooks pass as well.

Closes #1527
